Emotionally, she can stay regulated most of the time, yet gets easily pulled in by peer attention and the feeling that something is “secret” or “off-limits.”
scenario.childBackground: She is an 11-year-old Hispanic girl from a Mexican-American family; she speaks English at school and Spanish with her abuela. She lives with her mom and a younger brother in a small apartment, with her dad not living at home, and she spends a lot of after-school time online while her mom works late shifts. Money is tight but stable enough for a shared family phone plan and an older tablet, and most of her social life happens through group chats and social apps.
scenario.narrative:
One evening after homework, she curls up on the couch with her tablet and opens a group chat with a few classmates and kids she follows from a gaming and meme community. The conversation drifts from funny edits to social media “rules,” and someone mentions that certain hashtags are “restricted” and don’t show up the same way anymore. A friend jokes that it’s because the tags are “too much,” and another says you have to type them in a special way or the app won’t show the “real” posts.

She feels a quick spark of curiosity, partly because everyone is acting like it’s insider knowledge. She starts searching the tags they mention, watching how the app changes the results—some searches show a warning message, some show only a few posts, and some don’t autocomplete at all. She tries small variations: adding extra letters, swapping characters, and using similar words, just to see what gets through. As the results shift, she notices more photos of adult influencers where the camera angle and poses draw attention to body shape, with captions and comments that talk about “curves” and “hot” looks rather than anything neutral.

She scrolls longer than she meant to, half confused and half intrigued about what exactly makes these posts “special” or restricted. In the group chat, she asks casually why some tags get limited and whether there are other ones that “don’t work anymore,” trying to sound like she’s just curious about the platform, not the images themselves. At the same time, she keeps tapping into similar-looking accounts and suggested searches, comparing what seems allowed versus what seems pushed into the “hidden” corners of the app.
